table.title: UAX #14 Table 1. Line Breaking Classes (excerpt)
table.html:
ClassDescriptive NameExamplesBehavior
Non-tailorable Line Breaking Classes
BKMandatory BreakNL, PARAGRAPH SEPARATORCause a line break (after)
CRCarriage ReturnCRCause a line break (after), except between CR and LF
LFLine FeedLFCause a line break (after)
CMCombining MarkCombining marks, control codesProhibit a line break between the character and the preceding character
NLNext LineNELCause a line break (after)
SGSurrogateSurrogatesDo not occur in well-formed text
WJWord JoinerWJProhibit line breaks before and after
ZWZero Width SpaceZWSPProvide a break opportunity
GLNon-breaking (“Glue”)CGJ, NBSP, ZWNBSPProhibit line breaks before and after
SPSpaceSPACEEnable indirect line breaks
ZWJZero Width JoinerZero Width JoinerProhibit line breaks within joiner sequences
Break Opportunities
B2Break Opportunity Before and AfterEm dashProvide a line break opportunity before and after the character
BABreak AfterSpaces, most sentence-terminal punctuationGenerally provide a line break opportunity after the character
BBBreak BeforePunctuation used in dictionariesGenerally provide a line break opportunity before the character
table.edits: first two groups (14 classes); italics removed

d1.purpose: Provide a compact reference to Unicode line-breaking classes, their names, examples, and behavior.
tasks: Look up a class abbreviation and read across to its meaning, examples, and behavior.
Compare related classes, especially where their break behavior differs.
Scan each section sequentially to understand the range of classes.
relations: Each class code identifies a named class; its examples illustrate the characters covered, and its behavior describes the line-breaking effect.
The full-width section labels group classes by their role in line breaking.
roles: Class is the row header and primary lookup key; it needs little width but must remain easy to scan.
Descriptive Name translates the abbreviation into a recognizable concept.
Examples connects the class to characters or character categories.
Behavior carries the explanatory prose and is central to comparison.
Column headers label the fields; section rows separate the two groups.
keep_whole: Class abbreviations and other short identifiers such as ZWSP, NBSP, and ZWNBSP.
Individual words and numeric or technical identifiers.
Short names and examples where space permits.
may_wrap: Long descriptive names at word boundaries.
Example lists between items or words.
Behavior descriptions at natural word boundaries.
The Descriptive Name header if the column is narrow.
same_scale: All class codes should have a consistent narrow field.
Names, examples, and behaviors should remain readable as peer fields, while their widths reflect their different content lengths.
Both section labels should read as full-width group headings.
d1.h_vs_v: The 719px limit requires wrapping: extra width for behavior reduces prose line breaks, while extra width for names or examples improves scanning and comparison in those fields. More wrapping increases row height, but can be preferable to fragmenting meaningful phrases or making the reference difficult to scan.

d2.purpose: Provide a compact reference to Unicode line-breaking classes and their effects.
tasks: Find a class by its short code or descriptive name.
Understand and compare the line-breaking behavior of classes.
relations: Each class code, name, examples and behavior belong to the same row.
The full-width section rows group classes by their role in the line-breaking rules.
Examples illustrate a class; behavior explains its effect on line breaks.
roles: Class is a narrow row identifier used for lookup.
Descriptive Name expands the identifier into a readable label.
Examples connect the class to familiar characters or character categories.
Behavior carries the explanatory text and is likely to need the most wrapping.
The column headers label the fields; the full-width rows mark section boundaries.
keep_whole: Class codes and character abbreviations such as ZWJ, ZWSP and ZWNBSP.
Individual words and identifiers in names, examples and behavior.
Numbers and punctuation attached to their semantic units.
may_wrap: Multiword descriptive names at word boundaries.
Example lists between items or words.
Behavior descriptions at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The descriptive name and examples columns should have comparable prominence, though their widths can differ according to the chosen reading priority.
All class codes should share a compact, consistent lookup column.
Both section labels should read as full-width group headings.
d2.h_vs_v: The 719px limit requires some prose to wrap. Giving more width to behavior can reduce repeated line breaks, while wider names or examples can make scanning those fields easier at the cost of taller behavior cells.

d3.purpose: Provide a reference for Unicode line-breaking classes, their descriptive names, examples, and behavior.
tasks: Find a class by its short code or descriptive name.
Identify examples belonging to a class.
Compare the line-breaking behavior of related classes.
relations: Each data row connects one class code with its name, examples, and behavior.
Full-width group rows organize classes by their role in line breaking.
roles: Column headers identify the four fields.
Class codes are compact row labels used for lookup.
Descriptive names identify the classes in words.
Examples illustrate each class; behavior explains its effect on line breaks.
Group labels span the table and separate sections.
keep_whole: Class codes and abbreviations, including ZWJ and ZWNBSP.
Individual words and hyphenated or otherwise unbreakable units.
Numbers and identifiers within the behavior text.
may_wrap: Descriptive names at natural word boundaries.
Lists of examples between items or at natural word boundaries.
Long group labels at natural word boundaries if needed.
same_scale: All class codes should have the same narrow column.
Names and examples serve parallel identification tasks and can have comparable space, although their content lengths differ.
Behavior descriptions are longer prose and can warrant more width than the identification columns.
d3.h_vs_v: The table must fit within 719px. Giving more width to behavior reduces prose wrapping, while giving more to names or examples improves lookup; the resulting extra row height is acceptable where text remains easy to scan.

analysis.strengths: All content is visible, headers remain on one line, and no words are broken internally. The compact class column supports scanning, while the wide behavior column keeps several definitions on one line.
analysis.faults: The BA example splits “sentence-terminal” at the hyphen, and the BK example separates “PARAGRAPH” from “SEPARATOR.” Several two-line rows leave considerable empty space in their shorter cells.
analysis.spatial_logic: The class column is kept to its minimum useful width. The remaining space favors behavior, with smaller allocations to descriptive names and examples.

analysis.strengths: It preserves the same clear structure, legibility, row heights, and two-line maximum as P. Its slightly wider descriptive-name column gives that field a little more room.
analysis.faults: The extra four pixels do not visibly improve the name wrapping, while the same example phrases remain split. Its behavior column is slightly narrower without an apparent compensating benefit.
analysis.spatial_logic: Q shifts four pixels from behavior to descriptive names, leaving the class and examples columns unchanged. In the rendered table, that small adjustment produces no meaningful improvement in the line breaks.

rounds.insights: P and Q are effectively tied in the rendered result: their small width difference does not change the table’s height or visible wrapping. The most promising adjustment is to give examples more room, since that column splits several meaningful phrases, while keeping enough width in behavior to preserve its useful single-line entries. Any proposed allocation needs rendering to confirm its actual breaks.

analysis.strengths: All headers fit on one line, and the wider Examples column gives its entries room to breathe. Class codes and section divisions are easy to scan.
analysis.faults: The CM behavior runs to three lines, and the GL descriptive name wraps, creating taller rows than in P and Q. The BA example breaks at the hyphen in “sentence-terminal.”
analysis.spatial_logic: Examples receives space that would be more useful in Behavior and Descriptive Name; the resulting height changes interrupt the table’s rhythm.

analysis.strengths: The wider Behavior column reduces CM to two lines, while the wider Descriptive Name keeps GL on one line. All cells remain at two lines or fewer, with clear section bands and intact headers.
analysis.faults: The BA example still breaks at the hyphen in “sentence-terminal.” Several behavior statements wrap, although their breaks remain readable.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow class column supports lookup, while the largest share goes to the sentence-length behavior descriptions. The remaining space balances names and examples effectively.

analysis.strengths: Like P, it keeps the GL name on one line and limits cells to two lines. Its headers, section bands and class codes remain easy to scan.
analysis.faults: The BA example has the same hyphen break as P. The additional four pixels in Descriptive Name produce no visible improvement over P, while slightly narrowing Behavior.
analysis.spatial_logic: Its proportions and row rhythm closely match P; the small shift toward names does not visibly improve the reading experience.

rounds.insights: A modest transfer of width from Examples to Descriptive Name and Behavior removes two costly wraps without introducing additional lines elsewhere. P and Q render almost identically; P gives the longer behavior prose slightly more room. The remaining hyphen break in BA occurs in both layouts and would require a consequential width trade-off to address.

contrast.why: Equalizing the three text columns leaves Behavior too narrow for its long explanations, causing more wrapping and taller rows while giving unnecessary space to shorter names and examples. This contrast is a width proposal, not a rendered candidate.

synthesis.rationale: Layout P keeps the class codes compact and gives the most space to the explanatory Behavior column, while all headers remain on one line and cells stay within two lines. Layout Q produces essentially the same wrapping and is also publishable, but its four-pixel shift toward names offers no visible advantage. In s0B, the wider Examples column comes at the cost of a three-line CM explanation and a wrapped GL name, making the table taller and less even.

general: Allocate width according to content and reading task rather than making columns equal by default.
Assess actual line breaks and row relationships alongside clipping and word integrity.
specific: Keep the Class column just wide enough for its header and codes.
Give Behavior enough room for its longer explanations while preserving usable widths for names and examples.

synthesis.tradeoffs: P and Q still split some examples across lines, including the hyphenated sentence-terminal compound. s0B gives examples more room, but the visible gain does not offset its extra wrapping in names and behavior.
synthesis.uncertain: P and Q are nearly indistinguishable in the supplied renders; their ranking is a small editorial preference. The contrast layout has not been rendered.
